summary: Astrobotic's Griffin-1, designated NASA's Moon Base II, is targeted to launch no earlier than November 2026 on a Falcon Heavy from Kennedy Space Center, carrying 10 payloads representing six countries — five of them NASA's — to Nobile Crater near the lunar south pole. The manifest includes Astrolab's roughly 500 kg FLIP (FLEX Lunar Innovation Platform) rover in the slot vacated by VIPER, Voyager's own CubeRover, the BEACON payload flown with Mission Control of Canada, and ESA's LandCam-X. title: Falcon 9 upper stage from the Blue Ghost 1 launch impacts the Moon
summary: The roughly four-tonne Falcon 9 upper stage from the January 15, 2025 launch of Firefly's Blue Ghost 1 and ispace's Resilience landers struck the Moon near Einstein crater on the western limb at about 06:35 UTC on August 5, 2026. The impact was unintentional: the stage was passivated after launch but could not be deorbited on a high-energy trajectory, and solar activity plus gravitational perturbations later put it on a lunar collision course. Independent astronomer Bill Gray first reported the projected impact in April 2026 and NASA's Center for Near Earth Object Studies confirmed it; NASA's Meteoroid Environments Office attempted ground-based observation of a roughly two-to-three-tonne TNT equivalent event.

summary: After NASA and Draper ended CLPS task order CP-12 in July 2026, ispace's Mission 5 — the mission formerly numbered ispace-U.S. Mission 3, and the flight CP-12 would have used — is being pursued as a commercial ULTRA lander mission in 2029. ispace's Q1 FY2027 materials of August 7, 2026 state that "CP-12 has ended" and that the company "continues M5 targeting lunar landing mission in 2029" while actively pursuing new contracts, citing infrastructure and security demand across Japan, the United States and Europe.

summary: In its Q1 FY2027 materials of August 7, 2026 ispace announced a new lunar transport service built on a secured 500 kg payload allocation aboard a SpaceX Starship targeting a lunar landing as early as 2030, sold through an in-house "Mobile Cargo System" that provides comprehensive services for payloads under 500 kg including integration and operational support. ispace frames the arrangement as an evolution into a "Lunar Access Integrator" offering end-to-end integration, transportation and operations from Earth to the lunar surface alongside its own ULTRA landers, and began global sales when the service was announced.

title: NASA directs a simplified AxEMU "Sortie Suit" for the first landings
summary: NASA decided in early September 2026 to develop a simplified "Sortie Suit" variant of Axiom Space's AxEMU for the initial Artemis surface missions, announced at an internal meeting at the direction of Artemis program manager Jeremy Parsons. The stated goals are lower suit mass, reduced complexity and simpler interfaces between the suit and the landers, with the variant intended for the first landings flown on vehicles from both SpaceX and Blue Origin and capability added over time as surface experience accumulates. At the same week's Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel meeting, panel member Charlie Precourt said NASA leadership was meeting Axiom six days a week and that "requirements are being adjusted to reflect near-term mission needs, including shortening the spacesuit certification duration requirements."

title: ESA selects its first small lunar missions (Terrae Novae)
summary: Under its Terrae Novae exploration programme ESA called for small, low-cost lunar missions capped at a development cost target of €50M and less than four and a half years from feasibility kick-off to launch, aiming to fly the first pilots between 2028 and 2030. Eight proposals were selected: seven received €150,000 each to mature their concepts — including SER3NE, LUREPOS, MOONRAKER, LUMI, LunPAN and the Danish-led Máni mapping satellite — while MAGPIE, the only proposal targeting a landing, was put on a direct implementation path toward a surface mission by the end of the decade. ESA member states approved the work plan for the prioritised missions on December 16, 2025, advancing seven concepts into the next phase after the nine-month studies completed.

title: Máni — Danish-led ESA lunar polar mapping satellite
summary: Máni, named for the Norse personification of the Moon, is a small ESA satellite led by the University of Copenhagen that will orbit over the lunar north and south poles and build high-resolution imagery and detailed 3D maps of the surface, so that future crews and rovers can land and traverse more safely. ESA member states approved the work plan including Máni on December 16, 2025 during the 342nd Council, advancing it to Phase A/B1 as one of seven concepts to progress, with launch planned for 2029. Space Inventor of Denmark is the prime industrial partner building the spacecraft, integrating instruments and components from Polish, Dutch and Slovenian suppliers, while a French team supplies data-processing software and helps select areas of interest; the full mission budget is around €50M.

title: Russian Academy of Sciences approves Russia's ILRS segment concept
summary: Roscosmos head Dmitry Bakanov told Russia's Federation Council on April 1, 2026 that the Russian Academy of Sciences had approved the concept for creating Russia's national segment of the China-led International Lunar Research Station. Russia's headline contribution remains a lunar power plant, agreed with CNSA in a May 2025 memorandum and contracted to NPO Lavochkin in December 2025. Lavochkin's published station work spans a lunar relay satellite, a lunar research satellite, a telecommunications module, robotic mobile modules for assembly and repair, energy modules, stationary science and technology modules, and a mobile research laboratory with an ascent rocket.
